overview:
In Jain philosophy, **pudgala** (often called *pudgalastikaya* when emphasizing its extension) is the fundamental category of matter and material energy. It is one of the six eternal substances (*ṣaḍ-dravya*) that constitute reality: *jīva* (soul), *pudgala* (matter), *dharma* (medium of motion), *adharma* (medium of rest), *ākāśa* (space), and *kāla* (time). Pudgala belongs to the class of *ajīva* (non-soul) and is the only substance that is directly perceptible by the senses. It is characterized by possessing color (*varṇa*), taste (*rasa*), smell (*gandha*), and touch (*sparśa*), and thus is described as *rūpī* (having form) and *mūrta* (corporeal). While pudgala undergoes infinite modifications, its fundamental status as a substance is beginningless and endless.

Etymologically, the word *pudgala* is commonly explained as deriving from the verbal roots *pur* (or *pūr*) meaning “to fill, to combine, to add” and *gal* meaning “to disintegrate, to dissolve, to separate.” On this basis, Jain philosophers define pudgala as that which is continually undergoing processes of aggregation and disaggregation—coming together into compounds and breaking apart into simpler forms. This dynamic of combination (*pūraṇa*) and disintegration (*galana*) is not a creation or annihilation of substance, but a ceaseless transformation of modes (*paryāya*) within an eternal substratum (*dravya*). Thus, pudgala exemplifies the Jain doctrine that every substance simultaneously exhibits origination (*utpāda*), destruction (*vyaya*), and permanence (*dhrauvya*).

Ontologically, pudgala is described as an *astikāya*—a substance with innumerable spatial units (*pradeśa*), extending throughout portions of the universe (*loka*). Its smallest indivisible unit is the *paramāṇu*, a subtle, non-sensory particle that cannot be further divided. Aggregates of paramāṇus form *skandha* (clusters or bodies of matter), which range from extremely subtle forms (such as karmic matter associated with the soul) to gross, visible objects like mountains, bodies, and everyday physical things. Classical texts classify pudgala in multiple ways: by grossness (very gross, gross, subtle, very subtle), by touch (two-touch, four-touch, eight-touch), by function (e.g., body-making matter, speech-organ matter, karmic matter), and by its relation to the soul (living, *prayoga-pariṇata*; non-living, *visrasa-pariṇata*).

A central doctrinal role of pudgala appears in the theory of karma. Jainism understands karmic bondage not as a purely moral or psychological metaphor, but as a real, subtle material attachment of pudgala to the soul. Karmic particles (*karma-pudgala*) are a special class of extremely subtle matter that are attracted to the soul through activities of mind, speech, and body (*yoga*). When these particles flow toward the soul (*āśrava*) and become bound (*bandha*), they obscure the soul’s innate qualities of infinite knowledge, perception, energy, and bliss. The spiritual path is therefore described as a process of stopping the inflow of new karmic pudgala (*saṃvara*) and shedding the already bound karmic matter (*nirjarā*), culminating in complete separation of soul and pudgala at liberation (*mokṣa*).

Jain thinkers emphasize that pudgala exists in both visible and invisible forms. Anything that is visible and tangible is necessarily pudgala, but not all pudgala is visible. Subtle forms include the matter that constitutes various bodies (*śarīra*)—such as the gross physical body, the protean body, the luminous body, and the karmic body—as well as the material basis of speech and thought. In canonical and later texts, detailed accounts are given of *vargaṇā* (streams or fields of matter) that supply the material for bodies, sense organs, and karmic bondage. These vargaṇās are specific modes of pudgala that interact with the soul in complex ways, forming the basis of embodiment and experience.

From the standpoint of sensory qualities, pudgala is defined by four fundamental attributes: color, taste, smell, and touch. Each of these has numerous varieties, giving rise to the immense diversity of material forms. For example, touch is further analyzed into categories such as hot, cold, smooth, rough, light, heavy, soft, hard, and more; combinations of these touches are used to classify different types of pudgala. This analysis is not merely descriptive but is integrated into Jain cosmology and ethics, since the material constitution of bodies and environments influences the conditions under which souls experience pleasure, pain, and spiritual opportunity.

In contrast to many theistic or idealist philosophies, Jainism does not treat matter as illusory or as a creation of a deity. Pudgala is an eternal, real, and indispensable component of the universe. However, it is always non-conscious and lacks the intrinsic capacities of awareness and liberation that belong to the soul. The interaction between conscious *jīva* and non-conscious *pudgala*—especially in the form of karmic bondage—is the core drama of samsaric existence. Liberation is achieved not by annihilating pudgala as a substance, but by completely disentangling the soul from all forms of pudgala, particularly karmic matter, so that each remains in its own pure state.

Modern comparative studies sometimes relate pudgala to physical matter and energy in contemporary science, noting parallels such as the idea of fundamental particles, fields, and transformations. Yet Jain texts maintain their own distinct conceptual framework, in which pudgala is defined by sensory qualities, moral implications (through karma), and its role in the multi-bodied constitution of living beings. The doctrine of pudgala thus serves as a bridge between metaphysics, cosmology, ethics, and spiritual practice, providing a systematic account of how material reality coexists with and conditions the journey of the soul through the stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*).

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra (also called Tattvārthādhigamasūtra)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.translation:
“There are the astikāyas of soul and non-soul.
The pudgala-astikāya possesses color, taste, smell, and touch.”
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārthasūtra is a foundational, pan-sectarian Jain philosophical text that systematically presents the six substances and their characteristics. The sutras cited occur in the section on dravya, where pudgala is defined as the only astikāya endowed with the four sensory qualities. This passage is often used as the canonical basis for describing pudgala as rūpī (having form) and as the paradigmatic matter-substance.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasāra (Jīvakāṇḍa and Karmakāṇḍa)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Nemicandra Siddhānta Cakravartin
primary_sources.original_text:
पुद्गलद्रव्यं तु वर्णरसगन्धस्पर्शात्मकं।
तत् परमानुस्कन्धभेदेन बहुधा प्रविभज्यते।
primary_sources.transliteration:
pudgala-dravyaṃ tu varṇa-rasa-gandha-sparśātmakaṃ.
tat paramāṇu-skandha-bhedena bahudhā pravibhajyate.
primary_sources.translation:
“Pudgala-substance is indeed constituted by color, taste, smell, and touch.
It is divided in many ways according to the distinction between paramāṇu and aggregates (skandha).”
primary_sources.notes: Gommatasāra is a major Digambara text that analyzes the soul and karma in great detail. In its discussions of ajīva and karma, it elaborates the nature of pudgala, distinguishing between the smallest units (paramāṇu) and their aggregates (skandha), and explaining how karmic matter is a subtle form of pudgala that binds to the soul. The cited style reflects the doctrinal emphasis on sensory qualities and the paramāṇu–skandha distinction.

primary_sources.title: Sarvārthasiddhi (Commentary on Tattvārthasūtra)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Pūjyapāda
primary_sources.original_text:
पुद्गलशब्दः पूरणगलनयोः। पूर्यते गल्यते इति पुद्गलः।
नित्यत्वेऽपि परिनामवत्त्वात् पूरणगलनयोः प्रवाहो न विरमति।
primary_sources.transliteration:
pudgala-śabdaḥ pūraṇa-galanayoḥ. pūryate galyate iti pudgalaḥ.
nityatve’pi parināmavattvāt pūraṇa-galanayoḥ pravāho na viramati.
primary_sources.translation:
“The term ‘pudgala’ is derived from ‘pūraṇa’ (combination) and ‘galana’ (disintegration). That which is filled and dissolved is called pudgala.
Even though it is eternal, because it possesses transformation, the flow of combination and disintegration never ceases.”
primary_sources.notes: Sarvārthasiddhi is a classical Digambara commentary on Tattvārthasūtra. Here, Pūjyapāda explains the etymology of ‘pudgala’ and clarifies how its eternal nature is reconciled with constant change. This passage is frequently cited in traditional and modern expositions to support the standard etymological and doctrinal definition of pudgala.

primary_sources.title: Pravacanasāra (and allied Digambara texts)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Kundakunda
primary_sources.original_text:
जीवो पुद्गलेन बन्धं लभते कर्मरूपेण।
पुद्गलपरिणामोऽयं कर्म इति निगद्यते।
primary_sources.transliteration:
jīvo pudgalena bandhaṃ labhate karma-rūpeṇa.
pudgala-pariṇāmo’yaṃ karma iti nigadyate.
primary_sources.translation:
“The soul obtains bondage through pudgala in the form of karma.
This transformation of pudgala is what is called karma.”
primary_sources.notes: Kundakunda’s works, including Pravacanasāra, are central to Digambara doctrinal formulations. The cited style expresses the idea that karma is a specific transformation of pudgala that binds to the soul, highlighting the material nature of karmic bondage. While exact wording varies across manuscripts and translations, the doctrinal content is consistent: karma is pudgala, and its relation to jīva is one of bondage.

primary_sources.title: Śvetāmbara canonical tradition (e.g., Uttarādhyayana-sūtra, Niyamasāra, and doctrinal summaries)
primary_sources.author: Various Ācāryas; redactional committees
primary_sources.original_text:
पुग्गलओ रङ्गरसगन्धफाससंपन्नो।
एगं दव्वं णिच्चं, ण होइ तस्स उवणासो।
primary_sources.transliteration:
puggalao raṅga-rasa-gandha-phāsa-saṃpanno.
egaṃ davvaṃ niccaṃ, ṇ hoi tassa uvaṇāso.
primary_sources.translation:
“Pudgala is endowed with color, taste, smell, and touch.
It is one eternal substance; there is no destruction of it.”
primary_sources.notes: In Śvetāmbara Prakrit sources and later doctrinal compendia, pudgala is similarly defined as the matter-substance possessing the four sensory qualities and as an eternal dravya. The wording here reflects typical Prakrit formulations found in canonical and post-canonical texts, emphasizing both the sensory attributes and the permanence of pudgala as a substance despite its changing modes.

misconceptions.myth: Pudgala is only gross, visible matter like earth, water, fire, and physical objects.
misconceptions.reality: Jain texts explicitly state that pudgala exists in both gross and extremely subtle forms. Subtle pudgala includes karmic matter, the material basis of various bodies (such as the karmic body and luminous body), and streams of matter (*vargaṇā*) that are not directly visible. Anything visible is pudgala, but not all pudgala is visible; its range extends from paramāṇu to vast aggregates.

misconceptions.myth: Karma in Jainism is purely metaphorical or psychological and has nothing to do with matter.
misconceptions.reality: Classical Jain doctrine consistently describes karma as a specific kind of pudgala—subtle material particles that attach to the soul. These karmic particles are attracted by activities of mind, speech, and body, and they obscure the soul’s innate qualities. Liberation is defined as the complete separation of the soul from all karmic pudgala, not merely a change in mental state.

misconceptions.myth: Pudgala is created and destroyed over time, like objects that come into existence and perish.
misconceptions.reality: Jain metaphysics distinguishes between the eternal substance (*dravya*) and its transient modes (*paryāya*). Pudgala as a substance is beginningless and endless; what arises and perishes are its particular configurations and forms (skandhas, bodies, objects). The processes of combination and disintegration (*pūraṇa* and *galana*) are transformations of pudgala’s modes, not creation or annihilation of the substance itself.

misconceptions.myth: Matter and soul are completely independent, with no real interaction between them.
misconceptions.reality: While Jainism maintains a strict ontological distinction between conscious *jīva* and non-conscious *pudgala*, it also teaches a profound interaction between them, especially through karmic bondage and embodiment. Pudgala forms the various bodies and sense organs through which the soul experiences the world, and karmic pudgala binds to the soul, conditioning its states. Spiritual practice aims precisely at regulating and ultimately ending this interaction in the form of bondage.

misconceptions.myth: Pudgala is identical to modern scientific matter and energy, so Jain doctrine can be fully reduced to physics.
misconceptions.reality: Although there are suggestive parallels—such as the idea of fundamental particles, fields, and transformations—Jain pudgala is defined within a distinct philosophical and ethical framework. It is characterized by sensory qualities, its role in karmic bondage, and its integration into a multi-bodied conception of living beings. Modern physics does not recognize karmic matter or the moral dimensions of material interaction, so any comparison must be carefully qualified rather than treated as a simple identity.
